catalog_quote: Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. This fact further distances Lakes Plain languages from the Trans New Guinea Phylum. All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Duvle and Sikaritai have only these tones with Martin (1991) analysing the Sikaritai system as pitch-accent. The remainder of the languages also have combinations of high and low (or contours); Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991), Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi (Kim 1995) and all the western Tariku languages have a fall and a rise (Clouse n.d.1). new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level statement covering Tause: every Lakes Plain language (Tause included, with word lists in the same appendix) is tonal with at least H and L, and stress has not been found to be contrastive in any of them; no rule for the position of a (non-contrastive) stress is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. For tone: Duvle and Sikaritai have only H and L (Sikaritai analysed as pitch accent by Martin 1991); the western Tariku languages and Edopi add a fall and a rise; Iau has eight tones.
new_statements.domain_note: Comparative/reconstruction paper; the statement is about the whole Lakes Plain family, not a Tause-specific phonology. Tause data in the paper are survey word lists (Derapos, P. Munnings 1984 'after several years in the language'; Weirate and Deirate, D. Clouse 1992, survey) which are not tone- or stress-marked. Note that in sec. 8.2 (p.148) Clouse treats Tause as a daughter of Proto West Tariku, while his classification chart (p.155) lists 'Tause Family-Level Isolate' beside the West Tariku family, so whether the 'western Tariku' fall-and-rise statement is meant to include Tause is not certain. The text layer of the PDF reads 'modem' for 'modern'.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog taus1252 = Tause [tad], dialects Tause (Derapos), Weirate and Deirate. Clouse 1997 covers all three by word lists (Derapos list by P. Munnings 1984; Weirate and Deirate survey lists by D. Clouse 1992) and classifies Tause as a family-level isolate within the Tariku stock of Lakes Plain (Ross 2005 later moved it to East Bird's Head-Sentani on pronoun evidence; Usher keeps it in West Lakes Plains). The quoted statement is a family-wide generalisation over all Lakes Plain languages, not a Tause-specific description.
